title: Multimodal Microscopy to Study Poplar Stem Structures and Cell Walls
content: Microscopy has been pivotal in studying plant morphology, anatomy, cellular and subcellar structures, as well as any phenotypic changes at these multilevels resulted from mutation or genetic engineering. As microscopy continues to advance, the chemical fixation, sample preparations with microtomy and ultramicrotomy remain essential methodologies for plant biology research. Here we optimize protocols for poplar stem research using light and electron microscopy. Stem segments were fixed in glutaraldehyde and first cut with a vibratome. Sections stained with phloroglucinol showed the wood structures and lignin distribution at light microscopy (LM) level. Some thicker sections were dehydrated and critical point dried for scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging. SEM provided images with a range of magnifications and field of views. However, without infiltration of a supporting medium, certain structural distortions of vibratome sectioning could be seen at higher magnification. To image the fine cellular and subcellular structures, stem segments were post-fixed, dehydrated, infiltrated, and embedded in the Spurr’s low viscosity resin. Thin sections were prepared and stained with potassium permanganate or uranyl acetate/lead citrate. Transmission electron microscopy images provided fine structural details of different cell types, subcellular contents, the layers of secondary cell walls. Our data also indicated that uranyl acetate/lead citrate staining generated overall better contrast therefore offering high resolution of cell wall ultrastructural imaging. These protocols, especially for EM sample preparations, will have broader applicability since authors have been working on other species as well, such as Arabidopsis, fern, rice, and sorghum.
